While in your defensive stance, you can make a number of {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks} equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} without using your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, and you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to make a melee attack against a creature that moves more than 5 feet while within your reach.

entries.name: Sharpshooting
entries: You are skilled with {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons and can make shots that others find difficult. While you are wielding a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon with which you are proficient, gain a +2 bonus to ranged weapon attacks.

entries.name: Shielding
entries: You are skilled at using your shield to defend your allies as well as yourself. While you are wielding a shield with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When a creature you can see attacks a target other than you that is within 5 feet of you, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}.
If you are wielding a heavy shield, you are no longer required to wield a weapon with the light property in the other hand.

entries.name: Throwing
entries: You are skilled with the techniques of throwing weapons. While you are wielding a weapon with the thrown property with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to ranged attack and damage rolls.
Whenever you make a ranged attack with a thrown weapon, you can immediately draw another weapon as part of the attack.

entries.name: Two-Weapon Fighting
entries: You are skilled at fighting with two weapons. While you are wielding separate weapons in each hand, or a weapon with the double property, with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you engage in Two-Weapon Fighting, you can add your ability modifier to the damage of your Two-Weapon Fighting attack.
When you make an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}, you can attack with both of your weapons.

entries.name: Versatile Fighting
entries: You are skilled at using weapons in different ways. While you are wielding a melee weapon with the versatile property with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} while wielding a weapon in one hand.
You gain a +1 bonus to damage rolls while wielding a weapon in two hands.

entries.name: Fighting Masteries
entries: Certain class features or feats offer your choice of Fighting Mastery. Choose from the following. You can't take a Fighting Mastery option more than once, even if you later get to choose again.

entries.name: Brawling Mastery
entries: You've mastered using your weight to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, easily wrangling targets around. You gain the following benefits:

items: Your improvised weapons use a {@dice d6} for damage and gain the versatile (2d4) property.
Your unarmed strike damage increases by one step (from 1 to {@dice d4}, {@dice d4} to {@dice d6}, or {@dice d6} to {@dice d8}).
Your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} isn't halved by carrying a {@condition Grappled|sw5e-phb|grappled} creature who is the same size category as you or smaller.

Once per turn, when you hit a creature with an unarmed strike or an improvised weapon, you can make an additional unarmed strike or improvised {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack} against the same target without the aid of your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} (no action required).

entries.name: Close Quarters Shooting Mastery
entries: You've mastered getting up close and personal with {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons, maintain both rate of fire and accuracy. While you are wielding a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, you can choose to fire rapidly at the expense of accuracy. Your ranged weapon attacks are made without the aid of your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, but you use your {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to make an additional ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack}, also without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.
Your ranged weapon attacks ignore {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|half cover} against targets within 30 feet of you.

Other creatures provoke an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack} from you when they move to within 15 feet of you, and you can use {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons when making {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks}.

entries.name: Defense Mastery
entries: You've mastered the art of defending yourself, treating your armor as a second skin. While you are wearing armor with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: Critical hits made against you are treated as normal hits.
When a creature makes a melee attack against you and misses, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to attempt to shove that creature up to 10 feet directly away from you.

entries.name: Dueling Mastery
entries: Your mastery of fighting with a single melee weapon is unsurpassed; you make one weapon feel like many. While you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, you can decide to attack with haste at the expense of accuracy. Your melee weapon attacks are made without the aid of your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, but you use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to make an additional {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack}, also without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.

When a creature hits you with a melee attack, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to add your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to your AC for that attack, potentially causing the attack to miss you.

entries.name: Great Weapon Mastery
entries: You've mastered putting the weight of a weapon to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, letting its momentum empower your strikes. While you are wielding a melee weapon in two hands with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: On your turn, when you score a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} with a melee weapon or reduce a creature to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} with one, you can make one {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} as a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}.

Before you make a melee attack with a weapon that you are wielding in two-hands with which you are proficient with, you can choose to forgo your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. If the attack hits, you add double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to the attack's damage.

entries.name: Sentinel Mastery
entries: You've mastered techniques to take {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} of every drop in any enemy's guard; in tight spaces you are indomitable. While you are wielding a melee weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you hit a creature with an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}, the creature's {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} becomes 0 for the rest of the turn.
Creatures within 5 feet of you provoke {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks} from you even if they take the {@action Disengage|sw5e-phb} action before leaving your reach.

entries.name: Sharpshooting Mastery
entries: You have mastered {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons and can easily make shots that others find impossible. While you are wielding a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: Attacking at long range doesn't impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on your ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack rolls}.
Your ranged weapon attacks ignore {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|half cover} and three-quarters {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover}.

Before you make an attack with a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon that you are proficient with, you can choose to forgo your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. If the attack hits, you add double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to the attack's damage.

entries.name: Shielding Mastery
entries: You've mastered using a shield to defend your allies as well as yourself, and you understand that shields are not just for protection but also for offense. While you are wielding a shield with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: If you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action on your turn, you can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to try to shove a creature within 5 feet of you with your shield.

If you aren't {@condition Incapacitated|sw5e-phb|incapacitated}, you can add your shield's AC bonus to any Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} you make against a power or other harmful effect.

entries.name: Throwing Mastery
entries: You've mastered the techniques of throwing weapons, readily blending the weapons with your movements. While you are wielding a weapon with the thrown property with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} you make with thrown weapons.
Attacking at long range doesn't impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on your ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack rolls} with thrown weapons.

When you hit a creature with a ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack} with a thrown weapon, you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on your next {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} against that creature before the end of your next turn.
You can use Two-Weapon Fighting even when the melee weapons you are wielding in one hand aren't light, if at least one of them has the thrown property.

entries.name: Two-Weapon Mastery
entries: You've mastered fighting with two weapons, becoming a flurry of motion. While you are wielding separate weapons in each hand, or a weapon with the double property, with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: While wielding separate weapons in each hand, you gain a +1 bonus to AC.
While wielding a double weapon, when you roll a 1 on a weapon damage die, you can reroll the die and must use the new roll, even if the new roll is a 1.
You can engage in Two-Weapon Fighting even when the weapons you are wielding lack the light property.
You can draw or stow two weapons when you would normally be able to draw or stow only one.

When you engage in Two-Weapon Fighting, you can choose to forgo your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. If you do so, you can make an additional Two-Weapon Fighting attack, also without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.

entries.name: Versatile Mastery
entries: You've mastered the art of using weapons in different ways, altering your attack patterns mid-swing. While you are wielding a melee weapon with the versatile property with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you are the target of a {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack}, you can immediately use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to make a {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} against the target without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. On a hit, you impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} made against you.

If you miss an attack while wielding a weapon in two hands, you can immediately make an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} against the same target using one hand. You can only make this attack once per turn. If the two-handed attack was made with {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} or without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, this attack is made the same way.

If you miss an attack while wielding a weapon in one hand, you can immediately attempt to shove that creature up to 5 feet directly away from you. You can only make this attempt once per turn. If the one-handed attack was made with {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} or without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, this {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} is made the same way.

entries.name: Tactical Initiative
entries: Rather than each player character and creature acting on their own, two or more allied creatures can instead choose to act tactically and work together using this {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} variant rule.

entries.name: Rolling Tactical Initiative
entries: When combat begins and {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} would be rolled, two or more allied creatures can choose to work as a unit, provided they can see or hear and understand each other. When they do so, they each roll {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} separately, adding any modifiers as appropriate. Once each individual party has rolled their {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative}, the group then acts using the lowest result. Once a tactical group is formed, each character's {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} is set to the lowest result, even if the tactical group separates.

For instance, if three players want to use tactical {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative}, and they roll a 17, an 11, and a 14, all three players will instead act on {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} 11.

entries.name: Multiple Tactical Groups
entries: The party can use multiple tactical groups rather than all working in concert. For instance, a party of five might split into a tactical group of three and a tactical group of two, each group rolling their tactical {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} separately. A character can only belong to one tactical group at a time.

entries.name: Acting in Concert
entries: When a tactical group's turn comes up in the {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} order, each member of the group acts together. Their turns and actions can come in any order, though each individual tactical group member is still limited to what actions they could normally take. Additionally, actions that could normally be broken up, such as when a fighter takes the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action and has the Extra Attack feature, can be broken up during the turn.

For instance, a 5th-level fighter might take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action and make their first attack. Before they make their second attack, however, the operative ally in their tactical group might then take the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action to grant them {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} before the fighter makes the second attack.

entries.name: Separating a Tactical Group
entries: When a tactical group loses contact with each other, or if the tactical group chooses to break up on their turn (no action required), the tactical group becomes separated. When separated, each member of the former tactical group acts on their own, though they retain the {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} of the tactical group. The order of any active members of the former tactical group acting on the same {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} is determined randomly.

entries.name: Alternative Armor
entries: Traditionally, {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb|armor class} is designed entirely for avoidance. While unarmored or lightly armored, that's dodging the attack entirely. In medium or {@filter heavy armor|items|type=heavy armor}, however, that's absorbing the attack on your armor in such a way that it deals no damage. If you want a different approach to armor, try this variant rule.

entries.name: Armor Class (AC)
entries: Base {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb|armor class} (AC), without consideration of any special traits, class features, or armor and shields, is always calculated as 10 + Dexterity modifier, with armor replacing or augmenting that base AC calculation. Using this system, your base {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb|armor class} is instead calculated as follows:
{@b Base AC} = 8 + your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} + your Dexterity modifier

entries.name: Damage Reduction (DR)
entries: Damage reduction (DR) is a static value that you subtract when you take damage if certain conditions are met. Certain features, such as the Defense fighting mastery or the absorptive armor property, grant DR that only applies when you take damage from weapons. DR is expressed as a number. DR provided by armor only affects damage you take as a result of being hit by an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, in the same way that AC only helps you avoid being hit by an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}.
If passive DR would reduce the damage you take to 0, you instead take 1 damage.

entries.name: Armor Class vs. Damage Reduction
entries: Instead of focusing solely on damage avoidance, this variant rule balances {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb|armor class} and damage reduction, to better emphasize how armor is used. Each type of armor affects your AC and DR differently, as shown below.

entries.name: Light Armor
entries: As normal, {@filter light armor|items|type=light armor} does not prohibit the maximum Dexterity bonus you can receive to your AC. However, if the {@filter light armor|items|type=light armor} had a higher base AC, extra AC instead becomes damage reduction (DR).

For instance, {@item Fiber armor|sw5e-phb|fiber armor} normally increases your AC to 12 + Dexterity modifier. If you have a Dexterity modifier of +3, while wearing {@item Fiber armor|sw5e-phb|fiber armor} you would have an AC of 15. With this variant rule, however, {@item Fiber armor|sw5e-phb|fiber armor} instead grants you DR of 2 while allowing you to add your Dexterity modifier to your AC. If you have a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2, you would have an AC of 13 (8 + your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2 and your Dexterity modifier of +3) and DR of 2.

entries.name: Medium Armor
entries: {@filter medium armor|items|type=medium armor} strikes a balance between AC and DR. As normal, it still allows you to add up to +2 to your AC if your Dexterity modifier is +2 or higher.

For instance, {@item Weave armor|sw5e-phb|weave armor} normally increases your AC to 14 + Dexterity modifier (max 2). If you have a Dexterity modifier of +2 or higher, while wearing {@item Weave armor|sw5e-phb|weave armor} you would have an AC of 16. With this variant rule, however, {@item Weave armor|sw5e-phb|weave armor} instead grants you DR of 4 while allowing you to add your Dexterity modifier (max 2) to your AC. If you have a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2, you would have an AC of 12 (8 + your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2 and your Dexterity modifier of +2) and DR of 4.

entries.name: Heavy Armor
entries: {@filter heavy armor|items|type=heavy armor} focuses entirely on DR. You gain no benefit to AC from your Dexterity modifier, but you also aren't penalized if your Dexterity modifier is negative.

For instance, {@item Assault armor|sw5e-phb|assault armor} normally increases your AC to 17. With this variant rule, however, {@item Assault armor|sw5e-phb|assault armor} instead grants you DR of 7, but it grants no benefit to your AC. If you have a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2, you would have an AC of 10 (8 + your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2) and DR of 7.

entries.name: Unarmored Defense and Natural Armor
entries: Certain species (such as wookie or colicoid), classes (such as monk or berserker), or archetypes (such as {@book Blademaster Specialist|sw5e-ec|1|Blademaster Specialist} fighter) grant unarmored defense or natural armor. When using this variant, the following rules apply.

{@b {@i Unarmored Defense.}} If your unarmored defense includes Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence, Wisdom, or Charisma, you add that modifier to your AC as normal. If your unarmored defense includes your Constitution modifier, however, you instead treat that modifier as DR. For instance, a monk with a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2, a Dex modifier of +4, and a Wisdom modifier of +3 would have an AC of 17. A berserker with a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2, a Dex modifier of +4, and a Constitution modifier of +3, however, would have an AC of 14 and DR of 3.

{@b {@i Natural Armor.}} If your natural armor includes an adjustment to your base AC, that adjustment instead becomes DR. If your natural armor allows you to add your Dexterity modifier to your AC, you still add it as normal. For instance, a wookiee's hide grants them a base AC of 13 + Dexterity modifier. If the wookiee has a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2 and a Dexterity modifier of +2, instead of having an AC of 15 they would have an AC of 12 and DR of 3. A colicoid, however, who would have an AC of 17, with a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2, would have an AC of 10 and a DR of 7.

entries.name: Shields
entries: As normal, shields add their bonus to AC.

entries.name: Enhanced Items
entries: If an enhanced armor would add an additional bonus to AC, it instead increases DR. If an enhanced shield would add an additional bonus to AC, it continues to do so. If that bonus only applies to melee or ranged AC, it still only applies to melee or ranged AC or DR, as appropriate.

entries.name: Other AC Calculations
entries: Work with your GM to determine how other AC calculations, such as the {@i battle precognition} power or Way of Endurance consular's Upheld by the Force feature, should translate using these rules.

entries.name: Aging
entries: Sometimes, campaigns might take place over years, or even decades. As these campaigns progress, you might want to introduce mechanics to reflect your characters' natural aging. Alternatively, at character creation, you might want to create a character who is already at a later stage in life. Regardless of when your characters have aged, consider using the following variant rule.

entries.name: Aging Thresholds
entries: Every species ages at a different rate. While many near-human species age at the same rate as humans, reaching adulthood in their late teens, middle age in their 40's, elderly in their late 50's to early 60's, and venerability in their 70's, other species age differently. For instance, lanniks reach adulthood in their 50's and can live up to 900 years, while hutts aren't considered adults until they reach 200 years old and can live to be over a thousand.

Consequently, rather than tying aging to numbers, we instead establish three thresholds: Middle-Age, Elderly, and Venerable. Each time a character reaches one of these thresholds, they gain one or more aging quirks and one or more aging boons, determined by the threshold they've reached. When they do so, the GM can determine choose which quirk and boon they get, or determine it randomly, using the Aging Quirks and Aging Boons tables below:

rows: Your Strength score decreases by 1. Your maximum for this score decreases by 1.
Your Dexterity score decreases by 1. Your maximum for this score decreases by 1.
Your Constitution score decreases by 1. Your maximum for this score decreases by 1.
Your base walking {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} decreases by 5 feet.

entries.name: Aging Boons

rows: Your Intelligence score increases by 1. Your maximum for this score increases by 1.
Your Wisdom score increases by 1. Your maximum for this score increases by 1.
Your Charisma score increases by 1. Your maximum for this score increases by 1.
You gain proficiency in a language, skill, tool, or weapon of your choice.

entries: These effects are cumulative. When a middle-aged character, who has one quirk and one boon, becomes elderly, they gain two more quirks and two more boons, for a total of three of each. Additionally, duplicates are only rerolled at separate thresholds. If, at middle-age, your Strength score decreased by 1, your Strength score could again decrease by 1 at elderly.

entries.name: Middle-Aged
entries: Most species enter middle age about halfway through their expected life. For humans and near-humans, this is typically in their 40's, while lanniks don't reach middle age until about 400 years, and hutts at about 600 years. When a character reaches middle age, the GM should choose one quirk and one boon. Alternatively, they can determine the quirk and boon randomly.

entries.name: Elderly
entries: Like middle age, at which age a species becoming elderly also varies. For humans and near-humans, this is typically in their late 50's to early 60's, while lanniks are considered elderly at about 600, and hutts at about 750 years. When a character becomes elderly, the GM should choose two quirks and two boons. Alternatively, they can determine the quirks and boons randomly, rerolling any duplicates.

entries.name: Venerable
entries: Venerable members of a species are rare and typically revered by the younger members of their species. Humans and near-humans become in their 70's, lanniks at about 750, and hutts over the age of 900. When a character becomes venerable, the GM should choose three quirks and three boons. Alternatively, they can determine the quirks and boons randomly, rerolling any duplicates.

entries.name: Additional Aging Traits
entries: Some species gain additional traits as they age. For instance, hutts have the unique special characteristic in that they never stop growing from birth to death. The GM can add quirks and boons as appropriate for members of those species.

entries.name: Force-Bond
entries: When two Force-sensitive individuals spend time together, they can develop a powerful connection through the Force. While bonded in such a fashion, the two individuals gain a series of boons, depending on the strength of their bond. However, if the bond is unwilling, the individuals risk corruption by the dark side of the Force.

entries.name: Developing a Bond
entries: When one creature wants to develop a bond with another, they must spend 1 hour meditating, which can be done during a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest},  while within 30 feet of a target that they can see. At the end of this meditation, the target must make a Charisma {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. The DC of this {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} is equal to the initiator's universal force save DC, and the target of this feature can choose to fail this save. On a failure, the two creature's develop a Force-bond.

entries.name: Valid Targets
entries: Only sentient creatures who can cast {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st-level or higher can develop a Force-bond, and a creature can only be bonded in such a way to one other creature a time.

entries.name: Strengthening a Bond
entries: In order to strengthen their bond, bond-mates must remain with a certain distance of each other, as shown below in the Bond Distance and DC by Tier table. They must spend one week times the tier they are trying to achieve. For instance, to progress from 1st to 2nd tier takes two weeks, while progressing from 2nd to 3rd takes an additional three weeks. This time does not have to be continuous; bond-mates can spend three days together, two days apart, and then four more days together to achieve 2nd tier.

entries.name: Bond Distance and DC by Tier
Bond Features
entries: At each tier, bond-mates unlock a certain feature. In order to benefit from these features, bond-mates must be within 10 feet of eachother. This distance changes as their bond strengthens, as shown above in the Bond Distance and DC by Tier table.
For instance, at 1st tier, the bond-mates must be within 10 feet of each other to benefit from their bond's features. At 2nd tier, however, they must only be within 30 feet of each other.

entries.name: 1st Tier
entries: Both bond-mates always know precisely where their bond-mate is in relation to them, regardless of whether or not they can see or hear them.

entries.name: 2nd Tier
entries: Both bond-mates can speak with each other as if they were standing within 5 feet, provided they share a language. At 6th tier, this communication becomes telepathic.

entries.name: 3rd Tier
entries: Both bond-mates are constantly under the effects of the {@i sense emotions} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, but they are only able  to read each other's emotions. This does not require    {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} for either bond-mate, and this       feature can not be interrupted while both         bond-mates are conscious.

entries.name: 4th Tier
entries: As an action on each of their turns, bond-mates can pass items to each other. When a bond-mate uses their action in such a way, the other bond-mate must use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to take the item.

entries.name: 5th Tier
entries: Whenever a bond-mate makes an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} or {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} due to the other bond-mate taking the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action, they can reroll one of the dice once.

entries.name: 6th Tier
entries: When a bond-mate casts a {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, they can cast it as if they are standing within 5 feet of their bond-mate. If the power requires a target, and that target is not their bond-mate, they must be aware of the target's presence and location in order to target them with this power.

entries.name: 7th Tier
entries: When a bond-mate casts a power of 1st-level or higher that targets only themself, they can also target their bond-mate.

entries.name: 8th Tier
entries: Whenever a bond-mate is reduced to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, but not killed outright, the other bond-mate can use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to cause them to drop to 1 hit point instead.
Once this feature has been used, neither bond-mate can use it again until they both complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: 9th Tier
entries: On their turn, one bond-mate can use their action to give their bond-mate an additional turn. If they do so, the targeted bond-mate immediately takes an additional turn after the current bond-mate's turn.
Once this feature has been used, neither bond-mate can use it again until they both complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: 10th Tier
entries: Whenever a bond-mate takes damage, the other bond-mate can use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to grant them resistance to the damage. If they do so, both bond-mates take the same amount of damage. Alternatively, when a bond-mate has {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} restored, they can use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to halve the amount of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. If they do so, the other bond-mate regains the same number of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. These features can be used a number of times equal to the bond-mate's combined Wisdom or Charisma modifiers (their choice, a minimum of once). All expended uses are regained when both bond-mates complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: Breaking a Bond
entries: Sometimes, creatures might want to end their Force-bond, whether the bond was created unbeknownst to them or they no longer wish to share the bond. To do so, one of the creatures must spend 10 minutes meditating on the bond, and then make a Charisma {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. The DC of this {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} varies, depending on the tier of the bond, as shown above in the Bond Distance and DC by Tier table. On a success, the bond's tier is reduced by 1. If the bond's tier is 1, it is broken. On a failure, the bond's tier is not reduced, and you can't try again for 24 hours.

entries.name: Crueler Criticals
entries: Normally, when you score a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit}, you roll the damage dice twice and add your modifier once. For instance, if you are wielding a weapon that deals 1d8 kinetic damage and is governed by Strength, on a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} you deal 2d8 + your Strength modifier kinetic damage. Sometimes, poor rolls lead to you doing {@i less} damage on a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} than a normal hit. For instance, you might roll two 1's on your 2d8, which with your +3 Strength modifier is only 5 damage. This feels lackluster.

With this rule, instead of rolling the damage dice twice, you instead maximize the damage once and then roll the second die. So, using the above example, instead of rolling 2d8 and adding your Strength modifier, you instead roll 1d8, add 8 for the maximum die roll, and then add your Strength modifier. This will make critical hits feel more impactful.

entries.name: Combination Weapons
entries: Some weapons—specifically {@filter lightweapons|items|type=martial weapon|category=lightweapon}—can be used in a variety of ways. For instance, the iconic scenes with Darth Maul using his {@item Doublesaber|sw5e-phb|doublesaber}, but with only one blade extended. Or more recently with Cal Kestis in Jedi: Fallen Order, where you could adjust from {@item Doublesaber|sw5e-phb|doublesaber} fighting to single saber fighting, or vice versa, on the fly. If you want the option to combine weapons in this fashion, consider the following variant rule.

entries.name: Weapon Combination
entries: Combining weapons requires three key components: the two weapons you want to combine, and the appropriate tools. Two weapons can only be combined by someone proficient with appropriate tools, as shown in the Item Specific Tools table in Wretched Hives.

entries.name: Valid Targets
entries: Only unenhanced weapons of the same type can be combined, and you can't combine weapons that already have multiple modes, such as the IWS or bo-rifle. For instance, a {@filter lightweapon|items|type=martial weapon|category=lightweapon} can only be combined with another {@filter lightweapon|items|type=martial weapon|category=lightweapon}, while a {@filter vibroweapon|items|type=martial weapon} can only be combined with another {@filter vibroweapon|items|type=martial weapon}.

entries.name: Combining Weapons
entries: You can only combine a number of weapons up to your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. Combining weapons takes one hour and requires an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} with the appropriate tools, as shown in the Item Specific Tools table in Wretched Hives. The DC for the check is determined by the number of weapons being combined, as shown below in the Combination/Separation DC by Weapons table.

entries.name: Combination/Separation DC by Weapons
entries: On a success, the weapons are correctly combined. On a failure, the weapons are not combined, and you must wait 24 hours before you can try again.

entries.name: Separating Weapons
entries: Separating weapons requires an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} with the appropriate tool, as shown in the Item Specific Tools table. The DC for the check is determined by the total number of combined weapons before separating, as shown above in the Combination/Separation DC by Weapons table.

On a success, the weapons are correctly separated. On a failure, the weapons are not separated, you must wait 24 hours before you can try again, and you must roll a {@dice d20}. If you roll a 1 on the {@dice d20}, one currently combined weapon is destroyed. The GM should determine which weapon is destroyed randomly.

entries.name: Combined Weapons
entries: Once you've combined two weapons, you can readily switch between each weapon by using your object interaction on your turn. The combined weapon's weight is equal to the total weight of each individual part, and each weapon uses the appropriate damage and properties as shown in its statistics in the Weapons table.

For instance, a 3rd-level character decides they want to combine a greatsaber and a {@item Doublesaber|sw5e-phb|doublesaber}. They have both weapons available, as well as a set of artificer's tools. After spending one hour, they make an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} with the tools, resulting in a 17. The weapons are successfully combined, and using their object interaction each turn, the character can switch from a greatsaber to a {@item Doublesaber|sw5e-phb|doublesaber}, or back again.

When the character reaches 5th level, they decide they want to add a lightwhip to the mix. They obtain a lightwhip, and attempt to combine it with their current weapon over the course of an hour with their artificer's tools. At the end of the hour, however, they only roll an 8 on the check, failing to combine the third weapon. They must wait until tomorrow to try again.

entries.name: Blasters
entries: Unlike light- and vibro-weapons, you can't combine multiple {@filter blasters|items|firearm=true}. Instead, you can integrate a {@item Wrist launcher|sw5e-phb|wrist launcher} attachment to a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true}, as long as the weapon lacks the fixed property. This attachment can fire all {@item Wrist launcher|sw5e-phb|wrist launcher} ammunition with a range of 20/40, or it can fire grenades with a range of 40/80. This attachment has a reload value of 2, it can have different ammunition types loaded simultaneously, and you can choose which ammunition you're using as you fire it (no action required). Each ammunition must be reloaded separately.

When you would attempt to combine an additional weapon, you can instead attempt to increase this attachment's reload property by making an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} with the appropriate tool and consulting the Combination/Separation DC by Weapons table.

entries.name: Dueling
entries: Dueling, be it with lightsabers or {@filter blasters|items|firearm=true}, is an iconic experience in the Star Wars narrative. When you want to engage in a more narrative form of dueling, rather than traditional combat, consider the following rules.

entries.name: Opponents
entries: Most often, dueling is an event suited only to two people. It might be a fight to the death, a fight for honor, or simply a fight to see who is better. Alternatively, it might simply be a sparring session. These rules are intended to potentially encompass all of these possibilities, but only for a traditional one versus one encounter.

entries.name: Actions
entries: There are three major actions a dueling character can take: Attack, Defend, or Feint. During each round of dueling, each involved party must decide which of these three actions they will take.

entries.name: Attack
entries: The most common action, a character can choose to attack. When a character chooses to attack, they have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} during resolution if the opponent takes the Feint action, and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the roll if the character takes the Defend action.

entries.name: Defend
entries: The second action a character can take is is to defend. When a character chooses to defend, they have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} during resolution if the opponent takes the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the roll if the character takes the Feint action.

entries.name: Feint
entries: The third action a character can take is to feint. When a character chooses to feint, they have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} during resolution if the opponent takes the Defend action, and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} if the character takes the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action.

entries.name: Extra Attack
entries: If one party has the Extra Attack feature, and the other party doesn't, consider allowing them to roll with an additional instance of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}.

entries.name: Resolution
entries: Once each party has chosen their action, they should each make an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} as appropriate. The winner of the contest strikes a blow or scores a point, as appropriate.

entries.name: Ties
entries: Generally, ties should either award a point to both parties—or no points to either party—at the discretion of the GM.

entries.name: Strikes
entries: How many strikes a character can take varies based on the lethality of the contest. You might grant each party a potential three strikes if sparring, or you might give them each strikes equal to their Constitution modifier in a lethal contest, or even strikes equal to their {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} in a fight for honor.

entries.name: Overlapping Features
entries: Many species have features that make them better in certain martial ways: special traits like natural armor, armor and weapon proficiencies, or {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|sw5e-phb|unarmed strikes} and natural weapons. Counterintuitively, when those species choose certain classes, those features become obsolete instead of enhancing their class choice.
If you players choose such a species/class combination, consider using this variant rule.

entries.name: Armor Proficiencies
entries: Many species come with specific armor proficiencies suited to their species' culture, such as chiss or draethos, or natural unarmored defense, such as aing-tii or wookie. If a player chooses a species and class combination that would grant the same armor proficiencies, or a species with natural armor and a class with unarmored defense, consider instead granting them a bonus depending on the type of armor, as shown below:

items: {@b Unarmored Defense:} +1 bonus to AC while not wearing armor or wielding a shield.
{@b Light Armor:} +1 bonus to Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} while wearing {@filter light armor|items|type=light armor}.
{@b Medium Armor:} +1 bonus to Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} while wearing {@filter medium armor|items|type=medium armor}.
{@b Heavy Armor:} -1 damage taken from weapons while wearing {@filter heavy armor|items|type=heavy armor}. If this would reduce the damage to 0, the damage is instead reduced to 1.

entries: For instance, at 1st level, a draethos operative with a 16 in Dexterity would have +6 to Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} instead of +5 while wearing {@filter light armor|items|type=light armor}, while a wookiee berserker with a 14 in Dexterity and a 16 in Constitution would have an {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb} of 16 while unarmored, instead of 15. A character should only gain each bonus once.

entries.name: Weapon Proficiencies
entries: Many species come with specific weapon proficiencies suited to their species' culture, such as chiss or tuskens. If a player chooses a species and class combination that would grant the same weapon proficiencies, consider instead granting them a +1 bonus to damage rolls with the chosen weapon. For instance, at 1st level, a chiss scout with a 16 in Dexterity would have a +4 to damage rolls instead of a +3 when attacking with a {@item Blaster pistol|sw5e-phb} or {@item Sniper rifle|sw5e-phb|sniper rifle}. A character should only gain this bonus once, and this bonus does not apply if the species offers a choice of weapons, such as human or echani.

entries.name: Unarmed Strikes/Natural Weapons
entries: Many species come with higher unarmed strike damage, such as twi'lek or zabrak, or a natural weapon, such as chevin or karkarodons, representing their natural aptitude with unarmed combat. If a player chooses a species, class, or customization option combination that would both grant an increased unarmed strike, consider instead granting them a +1 bonus to their unarmed strike damage. For instance, at 1st level, a zabrak monk with a 16 in Dexterity would do 1d4+4 instead of 1d4+3 with their {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|sw5e-phb|unarmed strikes}. A character should only gain this bonus once.
Additionally, consider allowing those species that have natural weapons to use those weapons in place of their {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|sw5e-phb|unarmed strikes}, as appropriate.

entries.name: Situational Expertise
entries: Certain special traits, such as the aqualish Arms Dealer trait, give {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a skill in a certain situation. If you would already have {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in that situation, instead treat this feature as if it gave {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}.

entries.name: Compound Advantage
entries: Typically, multiple instances of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} don't stack; you either have it or you don't, and if you have both, you essentially have neither. This variant rule is designed to allow sources of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}—and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}—to stack, to a maximum of three times.

When you have two sources of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, you instead have {@b superadvantage}, which allows you to roll two additional d20s when you make your {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, or {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, and take the highest of the three dice. If you have three sources of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, however, you instead have {@b hyperadvantage}, which allows you to roll three additionals d20s and take the highest of the four. Consequently, if you have two sources of {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, you instead have {@b superdisadvantage}, and if you have three sources of {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, you have {@b hyperdisadvantage}, rolling three and four d20s, respectively, and taking the lowest.

Additionally, {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} no longer completely cancel each other out. Instead, if you have two sources of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} and one source of {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, you instead have one source of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}. For instance, if you are hidden from a creature, and an ally within 5 feet of it takes the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action, you would have two sources of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}—superadvantage—when you make your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}. If the creature is heavily obscured from you, however, you would have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, shifting you from superadvantage to {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}.

Each source of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} must be unique. For instance, if you are hidden from a creature, and an ally within 5 feet of it takes the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action, you would have two sources of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}—superadvantage—when you make your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}. If another ally also takes the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action, however, you still only have two unique sources of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, thus granting only superadvantage.

Some customization options, such as the {@feat Supreme Accuracy|sw5e-phb} feat, grant bonuses if you would have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}. If you elect to use this variant rule, adjust these customization options to instead grant an additional source of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} if you would already have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}. For instance, if you have the {@feat Supreme Accuracy|sw5e-phb} feat, if you have no source of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, you gain no benefit from the second bullet of the feat. If you have a source of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, however, the feat instead grants you superadvantage (or potentially hyperadvantage if you have an additional source of {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}).

entries.name: Passive Checks
entries: When determining your total for a passive check with this variant rule, if you have superadvantage on a check, add 8. For superdisadvantage, subtract 8. If you have hyperadvantage on a check, add 10, and if you have hyperdisadvantage, subtract 10.

entries.name: Careful Checks
entries: If you would have superadvantage on a careful check, you can instead take 18. If you have hyperadvantage on a check, you can instead take 20.

entries.name: Flanking
entries: When multiple creatures within 5 feet of another creature engage it in combat, that creature may become flanked. This variant rule offers mechanical boons to flanking separate from simple {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}.

A creature who is {@b one-quarter flanked} suffers a -2 penalty to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against sources within 5 feet of it. A creature is one-quarter flanked if it is at least one-fourth surrounded, either to a side, above, or below.

A creature who is {@b half flanked} suffers a -3 penalty to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against sources within 5 feet of it. A creature is half flanked if it is at least half surrounded, either to a side, above, or below.

A creature who is {@b three-quarters flanked} suffers a -5 penalty to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against sources within 5 feet of it. A creature is three-quarters flanked if it is at least three-quarters surrounded, either to a side, above, or below.

Alternatively, you can have players add a +2, +3, or +5 bonus to their {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} against creatures who are one-quarter, half, or three-quarters flanked, respectively, by them. Additionally, if you use the Saving Throws Checks variant, you can instead have them add a +2, +3, or +5 bonus to their Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} checks against creatures who are one-quarter, half, or three-quarters flanked, respectively, by them.

A creature who has a reach of greater than 5 feet gains the benefit of flanking against a creature while within melee range, but does not contribute towards flanking unless they are within 5 feet of the target.

{@b {@i Flanking on Squares.}} On a square grid, a Small or Medium creature takes up one square, and has eight squares surrounding it within 5 feet. When two or three of those squares are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is considered one-quarter flanked by those creatures. When four or five of those squares are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is considered half flanked by those creatures. If six or more of those squares are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is instead considered three-quarters flanked.

{@b {@i Flanking on Hexes.}} On a hex grid, a Small or Medium creature takes up one hex, and has six hexes surrounding it within 5 feet. When two of those squares are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is considered one-quarter flanked by those creatures. When three or four of those squares are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is considered half flanked by those creatures. If five or six of those hexes are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is instead considered three-quarters flanked.

Alternatively, you can run the simpler ruleset for flanking found in the DMG, that offers {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} instead of flat bonuses. That ruleset works alongside Advanced {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb} as well.

entries.name: Standing from Prone while Flanked
entries: When a creature attempts to stand from prone while flanked, it can choose to make a Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) or Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|sw5e-phb}) check (DC = 10 + its penalty from flanking). On a success, the creature stands and can move to an unoccupied space within 5 feet of it without provoking {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks}. On a failure, the creature remains prone and loses the movement it would have used to stand.

entries.name: Force Alignment
entries: The Force is manifested by two powerful and opposing aspects: the Ashla and the Bogan, more commonly known as the light side and the dark. As force-wielding characters evolve throughout the game, they can gravitate towards one side or the other (or neither, should they choose), resulting in physical manifestations and boons.

entries.name: Alignment Score
entries: How much a character embodies an aspect of the Force is calculated using their Alignment Score. The Alignment Score is an ever-shifting value falling between Light 100 to Dark 100. Characters gain an Alignment Score by gaining Light/Dark Points, as determined by their actions.

entries.name: Gaining Light/Dark Points
entries: When a character performs an act associated with one side of the Force, they gain points accordingly. Players can gain Light Points through a multitude of actions:

items: The first time you cast a light side {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st-level or higher, you gain Light Points equal to the power's level. Subsequent castings of that power earn you 1 Light Point.
Committing selfless acts, such as deliberately saving others at the expense of yourself, can earn you 1 or more Light Points.
Other benevolent acts, as determined by your GM, can earn you 1 or more Light Points.

entries: Consequently, players can also gain Dark Points through various actions:

items: The first time you cast a dark side {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st-level or higher you gain Dark Points equal to the power's level. Subsequent castings of that power earn you 1 Dark Point.
Committing truly heinous acts, such as harming or murdering an innocent, can earn you 1 or more Dark Points.
Other evil acts, as determined by your GM, can earn you 1 or more Dark Points.

entries: If a character has a score and performs an opposing act, instead of gaining points towards the other aspect of the Force, they lose them from their current score. For instance, if a player has 5 Light Points, and casts a dark side power of 4th level, they would have their Light Points reduced to 1. If the player instead casts a dark side power of 7th level, their score would shift to Dark 2.

entries.name: Alignment Tiers
entries: As you earn Light/Dark Points, you reach certain tiers of Alignment Score that manifest themselves in varying ways. If you ever fall below the Light/Dark Points threshold for a Major tier, you immediately lose that tier's benefits. You regain the benefits when you meet the criteria again. Minor tier effects are permanent unless another similar effect occurs.

entries.name: Minor Benevolence/Corruption
entries: At certain tiers of Light/Dark Points, you risk manifesting Minor Traits, as shown in the Force Alignment table. When you would earn a Minor Trait, you must first make a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} (Charisma for Benevolence, Wisdom for Corruption), the DC of which varies depending on the tier of the Minor Trait, as shown in the Minor Benevolence/Corruption Save DC table below. On a failed save, you must roll on a Minor Benevolence/Corruption tables, depending on the tier of the Minor Benevolence/Corruption. You can choose to fail this {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, if you wish.

rows: Your eyes tend to brighten during moments of satisfaction.
Your body is less likely to scar or show lasting signs of injury.
Your voice becomes slightly more eloquent.
Tame animals seem less uneasy around you.
Your eyes become more stark and vibrant.
Any existing scars on your body fade, and wounds never scar or fester.
Your voice gains a pleasant, melodic speaking cadence.
Your hair gains subtle highlights of gold or silver that occasionally reflect light.
Your eyes gain flecks of an unusual, complimenting color, such as amber or emerald.
Your skin always has a healthy tone.
You never suffer from minor illnesses, always appearing to be the pinnacle of health.
Wild animals become significantly less prone to attacking you.
Your eyes permanently take on an unusual, complimenting color, such as green becoming bright emerald.
Your voice has a naturally calming quality that puts others at easy.
You seem all but immune to naturally occurring illnesses.
Your hair takes on visible streaks of gold or silver.
Your hair begins to wither and fall out.
Your eyes permanently gain a faint glow.
You exude a calming presence that brings a slight feeling of peace to those around you.
Withered or sickly plants seem to liven in your presence.
You appear 1d10 years more youthful than you actually are. This does not change your actual life span.
Your eyes turn a pale yellow during moments of anger.
Your hair starts to lose its color, with gray streaks appearing throughout it.
Your eyes turn a luminous, sulfuric yellow with fiery red rims around the irises during moments of anger.
Any scars on your body become more noticeable, and your wounds become more pronounced.
Your voice lowers in pitch and becomes raspier.
Your eyes permanently turn a luminous, sulfuric yellow with fiery red rings around the irises.
Your skin begins to lose its pigmentation, becoming pale and mottled.
Your veins become increasingly visible across your entire body, as if they are sticking out.
Your hair loses its color entirely, turning a stark white.
Your eyes permanently turn a luminous, dark orange with fiery red rings around the irises.
Your skin loses its pigmentation, turning nearly stark white, while your veins become even more accentuated.
Your nails and claws begin to wither and grow longer, turning a vile yellow color.
Your hair begins to wither and fall out.
Your eyes permanently turn a luminous, blood red with fiery red rings around the irises.
You appear physically devoid of emotions. Your feelings never project outwards.
You develop a sickly, uncontrollable cough.
You appear 1d10 year older than you actually are. This does not change your actual life span.

entries.name: Major Benevolence
entries: At certain tiers of Light Points, as shown in the Force Alignment table, you manifest a Major Benevolence.

entries.name: Tier I
entries: When you or an ally within 30 feet of you makes a Charisma ({@skill Persuasion|sw5e-phb}) check to attempt to calm a creature or bring peace/alliance, you may spend a force point to add 1d4 to the result of the roll.

entries.name: Tier II
entries: When a friendly creature other than you within 30 feet that you can see fails a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} against being {@condition Frightened|sw5e-phb|frightened}, you can spend 1 force point to have them reroll the die. They must use the new roll.

entries.name: Tier III
entries: When an ally within 30 feet of you rolls a 1 on the {@dice d20} for an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} or {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, you can spend 1 force point to let the ally reroll the die. They must use the new roll.

entries.name: Tier IV
entries: Casting light side {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st level or higher costs 1 fewer force point, but casting {@book dark side powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st level or higher costs 1 more.

entries.name: Luminous Being (Tier V)
entries: You have become a physical manifestation of the light side of the Force, gaining one of the following boons. Your GM can choose the boon for you, or roll a die to determine it randomly.
{@b {@i Lightbringer.}} Your maximum force points increases by 10.

{@b {@i Protection.}} When a friendly creature other than you within 30 feet that you can see takes damage from any source, you can reduce that damage to 0. Once you've used this boon, you can't use it again until you finish a short or {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.
{@b {@i Immutable Defense.}} The damage resistances of friendly creatures other than you within 30 feet of you cannot be ignored.

{@b {@i Quick Casting.}} Choose one light side {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} you know of 1st through 3rd level that has a casting time of 1 action. That power's casting time is now 1 {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} for you.

{@b {@i Lay On Hands.}} You can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} and touch a friendly creature other than yourself, causing them to recover a number of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to half their hit point maximum. Once you've used this boon, you can't use it again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

{@b {@i Healer.}} If a friendly creature within 30 feet of you regains {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} at the end of a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} by spending one or more Hit Dice, that creature regains additional {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to your Wisdom modifier.

entries.name: Major Corruption
entries: At certain tiers of Dark Points, as shown in the Force Alignment table, you manifest a Major Corruption.

entries.name: Tier I
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on Charisma ({@skill Intimidation|sw5e-phb}) checks and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on Wisdom ({@skill Insight|sw5e-phb}) checks made against creatures with a higher Wisdom score than you.

entries.name: Tier II
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against being {@condition Frightened|sw5e-phb|frightened}, and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against being {@condition Charmed|sw5e-phb|charmed}.

entries.name: Tier III
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} made against dark side {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}. Additionally, when you receive healing from light side {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, you only regain half the amount of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}.

entries.name: Tier IV
entries: Casting dark side {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st level or higher costs 1 fewer force point, but casting {@book light side powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st level or higher costs 1 more.

entries.name: Dark Entity (Tier V)
entries: You have become a physical manifestation of the dark side of the Force, gaining one of the following boons. Your GM can choose the boon for you, or roll a die to determine it randomly.
{@b {@i Deathbringer.}} Your maximum force points increases by 10.

{@b {@i Invincibility.}} When you take damage from any source, you can reduce that damage to 0. Once you've used this boon, you can't use it again until you finish a short or {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.
{@b {@i Irresistible Offense.}} You can bypass the damage resistances of any creature.

{@b {@i Quick Casting.}} Choose one dark side {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} you know of 1st through 3rd level that has a casting time of 1 action. That power's casting time is now 1 {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} for you.

{@b {@i Recovery.}} You can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to recover a number of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to half your hit point maximum. Once you use this boon, you can't use it again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.
{@b {@i Power Mastery.}} Choose one 1st-level dark side power that you can cast. You can now cast that power at its lowest level without expending force points.

entries.name: Destiny
entries: Destiny plays a large role in the {@i Star Wars} universe. As a young boy, Anakin Skywalker is told that his destiny is to bring about balance to the Force. Padme's destiny is to give birth to the twins, Luke and Leia, so that they can fulfil their own destinies. Luke Skywalker learns that his destiny is to redeem his father, Darth Vader, so that balance to the Force is restored. Leia's destiny is to save the Rebellion from annihilation at the hands of the Empire and help forge the New Republic. The destiny mechanic helps players and GMs recognize that all heroes - and even major villains - have significant roles to play in the fate of the galaxy. Destiny rewards players for good roleplaying and gives GM new plot hooks to use when designing adventures.

The rules presented below are optional. A GM may decide to use Destiny Points or not; however, the decision to use them should be made before the campaign gets underway, so that each player can decide whether or not to embrace a destiny for their character from the outset.

entries.name: Choosing a Destiny
entries: Players don't need to choose destinies for their heroes at the start of the campaign - or ever for that matter. Not every hero has a destiny that must be fulfilled before the end of the campaign, and even players who want their characters to have destinies need to give their characters - and the campaign - a chance to develop first. It may take several adventures before players understand where the campaign is going and what goals their heroes are likely to pursue.

Choosing a destiny can be handled in one of two ways: either the player can select an appropriate destiny for their hero (based on what's happening in the campaign), or the GM can select a secret destiny for the hero. If the player chooses a destiny for their character, the GM should challenge the player to fulfil their destiny by presenting conflicting situations where the smartest and most beneficial decision might force the character to choose between doing what is best for their fellow heroes and taking steps towards their destiny. If the GM secretly chooses the hero's destiny, they must present challenges that let the character move closer to achieving their destiny, imparting benefits when the character is moving in the right direction and imposing penalties when the character does something that takes them far from the destined path. The GM-selected "secret destiny" forces the player to take their character through a period of self-discovery, as they learn which action leads them closer to - or farther from - their destiny. In essence, this mirrors Luke Skywalker's struggle at the end of {@i The Empire Strikes Back}, when he must choose between redeeming his father and falling prey to the corruption of the dark side.

A character with a destiny gains short-term benefits whenever they make significant progress towards fulfilling it, while a character who pursues goals that move them further away from their destiny suffers short-term negative effects. Conversely, a character without a destiny has nothing to gain and nothing to lose. A character may even fulfill one destiny and take on another.

The GM and players should work together to determine a destiny's impact on a campaign. One or more destinies might form the driving force for an entire campaign, or the central focus of a short series of adventures. In one of these cases, the GM should present the characters with choices that regularly affect their destinies, giving them many opportunities to gain destiny bonuses and penalties. Destiny-based campaigns should culminate in a final adventure that allows characters to ultimately resolve their destinies, for better or for worse.

entries.name: Destiny Points
entries: Destiny Points are a resource that a player can use to help fulfil whatever destiny has been set before their character. You either have a Destiny Point or you don't - you can't stockpile multiple Destiny Points for later use.

entries.name: Destiny Bonus
entries: When a character accomplishes a goal or performs a task that clearly moves them closer to fulfilling their destiny (GM's determination), they gain a Destiny Point.

entries.name: Destiny Penalty
entries: When a character does something that clearly moves them away from their destiny (GM's determination), they lose their Destiny Point if they currently have one. If not, the GM gains one Destiny Point to be used against them.
If the character makes steps towards their destiny once more, this GM Destiny Point should first be discarded instead of awarding the player with one.

entries.name: Final Destiny
entries: When the moment or encounter of a character's final destiny is upon them (GM's determination) their Destiny Point is not expended upon use and may be used repeatedly. Examples of such a situation include Luke Skywalker at the Battle of Yavin, or Revan upon facing Darth Malak onboard the Star Forge.

entries.name: Destiny Fulfilled
entries: When a character fulfils their destiny, they gain permanent benefits. Sometimes fulfilling a destiny has other effects as well; these are also covered here.

entries.name: Spending Destiny Points
entries: Spending a Destiny Point does not take an action and grants one of the following benefits:

items: Gain {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, or {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}.

Impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on an enemy {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, or {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} (even once the attack is resolved).
Act out of turn (thus changing your position in the {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} order).
Take damage that would otherwise harm another character within your reach.
Immediately gain 2 of a consumable class resource (rage, force points, tech points, {@book superiority dice|sw5e-phb|13|Superiority and Maneuvers}, or focus)

entries.name: Sample Destinies
entries: The following sample destinies should provide a starting point for any character wishing to take {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} of the destiny rules. Each destiny includes a brief description, with examples.

entries.name: Champion
entries: Your destiny requires your to become leader of a large and/or significant group or organization and successfully lead it through an extremely threatening event. Characters who have this destiny might or might not know of the group they are destined to lead. They must attain this goal through a mixture of training, charisma, experience and political maneuvering. The GM might want to divide this into two destinies: attaining leadership and leading the group through troubled times.

Examples of this destiny include Mon Mothma leading the Rebel Alliance, Darth Sidious gaining control of the Republic, Wedge Antilles leading Rogue Squadron, and Admiral Ackbar escaping Grand Moff Tarkin and eventually taking command of the Rebel Fleet.

entries.name: Destiny Fulfilled
entries: You receive a permanent 2 increase to your Charisma score.

entries.name: Sample Champion Destiny: Recruiting
entries: Your destiny is to convince an influential person or group to secretly aid or openly join the resistance effort on a planet or in a sector. The person or group must have considerable authority and resources, and thus be able to operate behind a thick wall of underlings and bureacracy. The group might be a far-reaching criminal organization that has agents, established rackets, transports, and {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} facilities throughout a sector. It could be a corporation that could lend its financial and material support to a local rebellion. Perhaps the hero encourages an influential military, government, or corporate leader currently serving the Empire to defect and aid the resistance. Convincing this entity to change its allied or neutral stance towards the Empire requires the hero to undertake missions to earn that individual's trust.

entries.name: Corruption
entries: Your destiny is to corrupt an individual, organization, or location. You may seek to turn a person to the dark side or indoctrinate a group of people in the ways of evil. Your destiny may also be to become corrupted yourself, either by another character, an organisation, or a series of life-changing events that unfold over time. The corruption should be a long-term goal requiring a great deal of time and effort.

Examples of this destiny include the Emperor's corruption of Anakin Skywalker, a dark force-wielder transforming a Jedi shrine into a temple of evil, or an Imperial officer convincing an Alliance cell to betray the Rebellion.
Additionally, a character's destiny may be to allow themselves to be corrupted by the dark side; their fall into darkness becomes the path to achieving this destiny.

entries.name: Destiny Fulfilled
entries: Increase two ability scores of your choice by 1 each. In addition, if you are using the variant Dark Side Corruption rules, consult the Dark Side Corruption table.

entries.name: Creation
entries: Your destiny requires you to create an object, machine, or other item of great power or significant use. You must use this item in support of another character's destiny, or in a future destiny of your own. Others might help create the actual item, so long as you lead and make a significant contribution to the effort. Pursuing this destiny might require you to seek out rare or restricted materials, expert advice, and adequate construction facilities or shops.
Examples of this destiny include Grand Moff Tarkin and the construction of the Death Star, Raith Sienar and the TIE fighter, and Walex Blissex and the {@i Victory}-class Star Destroyers.

entries.name: Destiny Fulfilled
entries: Once per {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest}, you or any ally within line of sight can take two actions in a single round while performing an action using the created object.

entries.name: Destruction
entries: Your destiny is to destroy a person or object, for good or evil. A Rebel agent's destiny might be to destroy a tyrannical Imperial Moff presiding over his home planet, while a darkside may be destined to destroy a powerful Jedi training site used to bolster the ranks of the Jedi order. The target of this destiny should be something very difficult to reach, either because it's heavily guarded or well hidden. Example of this destiny include Darth Vader's destruction of the Emperor, Lando Calrissian's destruction of the Death Star II, or A-wing pilot Arvel Crynyd's destruction of the {@i Executor}.

entries.name: Destiny Fulfilled
entries: Increase one ability score of your choice by +2.

entries.name: Discovery
entries: Your destiny is to discover a person, species, object, or location that was either previously lost or unknown to the civilized galaxy. This could be as simple as seeking out the remains of a long-dead hero, or as rare as finding a vergence in the Force. A scout's destiny might be to find a thus-far-uncharted world that helps solve a galactic crisis, while a scoundrel's destiny might be to chart a new route through th Deep Core, allowing the Rebel Alliance to sneak past the Empire's security web. The thing being discovered should be something that can only be found as the result of a long-term search or serendipitous events that only occure because the character long ago set down the path that would lead to that discovery.
Examples of thise destiny include Qui-Gon Jinn's discovery of Anakin Skywalker on Tatooine or Kyle Katarn's discovery of the Valley of the Jedi.

entries.name: Base of resistance
entries: Your destiny requires you to establish a hidden base that provides a safe haven and support for resistance fighters in a specific region. You might need to locate a new world that could accommodate a secret base or find a concealed facility on a known world from which dissenters covertly operate agains the Empire. You might need to gather allies and create secret support networks to maintain the base, supply it with equipment and weapons, and provide transportation for resistance forces. The scope of this destiny varies; it might be enough to establish a secret gathering place and a supply depot to aid resistance fighters in a single city, or it might require the construction of a major base to support operations in an entire system or even a sector.

entries.name: Destiny Fulfilled
entries: You gain a permanent +1 destiny bonus to {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}.

entries.name: Education
entries: Your destiny is to train or educate another being or group of beings in some way. In some cases, this could mean taking a young Padawan learner and molding them into an eventual Jedi Master, or it could mean training fresh-faced Rebel Alliance recruits and molding them into a crack team of SpecForce operatives. Characters with this destiny are not merely teachers providing mundane training. The education that this destiny demands must be of great importance to the galaxy, and should lay the groundwork for the beneficiaries of your tutelage to go on to fulfil destinies of their own. Only when the training is complete can this destiny be fulfilled, and the process should take months or years to complete.
Examples of this destiny include Obi-Wan Kenobi's training of Anakin Skywalker, Yoda's training of Luke Skywalker, or Grand Admiral Thrawn's training of Captain Pellaeon.

entries.name: Destiny Fulfilled
entries: You gain a permanent destiny bonus equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} on checks made with one class skill of your choice.

entries.name: Liberation
entries: Your destiny is to liberate a group, population, or region from Imperial domination. The focus of this destiny can range from a persecuted group - a small alien enclave, a remote town, or an orbital installation - all the way to a city, a starport, or even an entire planet. For instance, a hero might endeavour to free a planet's governing legislature, which has been previously relocated to a well-guarded penal camp by a hard-line Imperial governor to silence its dissenting view.
